t.3.75.1: You should not suspect me of wrongdoing, O noble one, for it was I who, forsaking the gods, chose you, O lord of the Niṣadhas.
t.3.75.2: But for the sake of finding you, brāhmaṇas went out everywhere, singing my words in verses throughout the ten directions.
t.3.75.3: Then, O king, a learned brahmin named Parṇāda came to you in Kosalā, at the dwelling of Ṛtuparṇa.
t.3.75.4: When the message had been properly carried by him and the reply likewise brought back, I hit upon this means of bringing you here, O Naiṣadha.
t.3.75.5: For apart from you, O lord of the earth, there is no one else in the world able to travel a hundred yojanas in a single day with horses, O ruler of men.
t.3.75.6: O lord of the earth, as truly as I have done nothing wrong even in my mind, so truly do I clasp these feet of yours.
t.3.75.7: This ever-moving Wind, witness of all beings, roams through this world; let him release my life-breaths if I commit sin.
t.3.75.9: The moon moves within all beings like a witness; may he take away my life-breaths if I commit any sin.
t.3.75.8: Likewise the sharp-rayed sun ever moves above the world; may he loose my life-breaths if I commit any sin.
t.3.75.10: These three gods indeed sustain the whole of the three worlds. Let them declare the truth as it is, or else let them abandon me today.
t.3.75.11: When this had been said, Vāyu then spoke from the sky: "She has not committed any sin, Nala; I tell you the truth."
t.3.75.12: O king, the abundant treasure of her virtue has been well guarded by Damayantī; we have been her witnesses and her guardians for three full years.
t.3.75.14: Bhaimī is a fitting match for you, and you for Bhaimī, O lord of the earth. You should have no doubt about this; be united with your wife.
t.3.75.13: And this incomparable device was contrived by her for your sake, for no man here other than you could travel a hundred in a single day.
t.3.75.15: And as Vāyu spoke thus, a shower of flowers fell, the drums of the gods resounded, and an auspicious breeze blew.
t.3.75.16: Seeing that most wondrous thing, O Bhārata, King Nala, the tamer of foes, then cast off that suspicion of his concerning Damayantī.
t.3.75.17: Then the lord of the earth put on that spotless garment, and, remembering the king of the Nāgas, he thereupon regained his own form.
t.3.75.18: Then, seeing her husband in his own true form, the blameless daughter of Bhīma embraced Puṇyaśloka and cried out aloud.
t.3.75.19: King Nala, shining as he had of old, embraced Bhaimī, and he also greeted his own two children with fitting affection.
t.3.75.20: Then the fair-faced one, laying his face upon her own breast, sighed, the large-eyed woman, overwhelmed by that sorrow.
t.3.75.21: Even so, her limbs smeared with dirt, the bright-smiling one embraced that tiger among men and stood for a long time, bathed in tears.
t.3.75.22: Then, O king, the mother of Vaidarbhī joyfully told Bhīma everything just as it had happened to Damayantī and Nala.
t.3.75.24: Then the two of them, together and joyful, O king, spent the night recounting all that had happened before and all that each had experienced while wandering in the forest.
t.3.75.23: Then the great king said: "Early in the morning I shall see Nala, after he has performed his purifications, reunited with Damayantī and having spent the night in comfort."
t.3.75.25: Then, in the fourth year, having been reunited with his wife, he, his purpose fully accomplished with all his desires, attained the highest joy.
t.3.75.26: Damayantī too, having regained her husband, was greatly refreshed, like the earth whose crops are half-grown when it receives water.
t.3.75.27: Thus reunited, her weariness dispelled, her fever calmed, her spirit swelling with joy, Bhaimī, her desire fulfilled, shone like the night with the risen cool-rayed moon.
